CROs cite faster startup timelines, regulatory predictability and tax incentives as reasons for growing interest in Australia. State investments in manufacturing, translational research and advanced therapies aim to expand that advantage into a broader biotech ecosystem. The question remains whether Australia can support drug development at broader scale.
Pricing pressures, combined with a volatile U.S. regulatory and government funding environment, have increasingly steered biotechs and pharma to pursue clinical studies in Australia, CROs told BioSpace.
Recent Australian government incentives to promote life sciences in states such as Queensland and Victoria have further underscored the country’s strong predictability profile, which appeals to international sponsors. Still, the impetus raises questions about whether Australia can evolve from a preferred trial destination into a broader biotech innovation hub.
Higher U.S. company interest
“Our inquiries are up about 25% on last year, and U.S. sponsors account for the vast majority of that increase,” said Dr. Sud Agarwal, chief medical officer of iNGENū, a physician-owned and led CRO headquartered in Melbourne.
The main reason for these queries is financial savings, Agarwal said, as an early-phase trial in Australia costs much less than in the U.S. Three factors contribute to this:
There is no IND requirement. This is only required if the trial moves back to the U.S.
Ethics and regulatory approval typically take four to six weeks.
A refundable R&D tax offset of up to 43.5% is available to eligible smaller companies.
“For a venture-funded company, this means more data per dollar and a readout that arrives in time for the next financing round,” Agarwal said.
U.S biotechs are becoming more risk-conscious amid funding constraints and perceived unpredictability at the FDA and National Institutes of Health funding, said Ryan Klein, vice president, business development, US and APAC at the U.S.-based CRO Resolian. Resolian has five labs in four continents, including Australia.
Particularly for early phase sponsors with a minimal cash runway, risk is a paramount concern, said Jerome Barley, commercial director at Melbourne-based CRO Avion Medical. Barley noted the interest from U.S. companies has ticked up but not overwhelmingly so.
That said, “Australia does provide predictability or certainty on top of that speed and quality,” Barley said.
Faster timelines, high scientific rigor
The regulatory expectations around data, safety and trial design are no different than other global regulators, Klein noted. Barley agreed, adding that while Australia removes the administrative burden and friction, it retains the scientific rigor, with filings accepted internationally.
Sponsors can often move from submission to first dosing in as little as eight to 10 weeks in Australia, Klein said. This is compared with an FDA review process that can take up to six months and, in some cases, prolong beyond eight months.
Even if U.S. regulatory and financial conditions improve, Australia’s competitive advantage will remain strong, Agarwal said. “As sponsors, investors and regulators become more familiar with Australia as a research destination, their confidence in the data and the process increases,” he said. “Familiarity leads to repeat use, and repeat use leads to more referrals.”
Strong tax incentive
The R&D tax incentive has been a stalwart Australian competitive advantage for years, Barley said.
Under Australia’s federal Research and Development Tax Incentive , intended to encourage companies to conduct R&D in Australia, eligible companies can claim either a refundable or nonrefundable tax offset depending on their size and structure.
For prerevenue small biotech companies, the tax offset means they can recover a significant proportion of the R&D expenditure. This effectively lowers the net cost of conducting the clinical trial in Australia, Klein added.
State government support
In addition to national incentives, state governments–Victoria and Queensland in particular–have also created a warm environment to attract companies, Klein said.
Victoria has built a mature life sciences ecosystem with outstanding hospitals, KOL knowledge, universities and biotechs, Barley said, as well as developing globally scaled manufacturing capability .
Agarwal pointed out that Victoria hosts about 30% of national trial sites and in 2025, invested A$5 million in industry-sponsored trials.
The Queensland government has been investing heavily more in translational research, Barley noted. The Translational Research Institute is a significant Australian-first initiative in ‘bench to bedside’ medical research. In July, the government announced the expansion of advanced cell and gene therapy capability. Queensland has also committed A$11.2 million toward a new 40+ bed Phase 1 facility in Brisbane, Agarwal said.
A true biotech hub?
Combined, these investments suggest Australia is pursuing a goal larger than becoming just a preferred location for early clinical trials. But is the country ready for a larger biotech and pharma presence?
Australia has focused recently on building its manufacturing capacities for Phase 2 and 3 studies for Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standards, Klein said. This is essential to compete on the global level.
Regardless, the remaining gaps include GMP capacity for cell therapy, mRNA and biologic, Agarwal said. In addition, there is missing data infrastructure for trial data across sites and a lack of workforce training for specialized roles.
Ultimately, Australia’s population of 28 million people limits recruitment for large or event-driven trials, Agarwal added. Sponsors are less likely to choose Australia for large Phase 3 and cardiovascular outcomes trials; rare diseases with very small patient pools, which need multicountry recruitment; and gene-modified products, because gene regulatory licensing adds time.
The next steps in Australia’s evolution as a life sciences market beyond attracting clinical trials should address several areas, Agarwal said. They include IP and company retention; bolstering manufacturing and analytical capabilities, including GMP, bioanalysis, radiopharmaceuticals and cell and gene therapy; and simplifying national governance.

Acura Reveals Bespoke ADX Created in Partnership With BMX Superstar Coco Zurita: the CZ-77 Concept
9 photos
Photo: Acura
The custom, one-of-a-kind 2026 Acura ADX CZ-77 Concept has been inspired by Vans' iconic sneakers, and comes with signature elements across the materials and design cues to properly honor the “legendary action sports brand.”
The premium brand from Honda has been pretty busy this month, but not with actual product reveals: they recently trademarked four new nameplates (TDX, LDX, Type-Trail, Type T) and confirmed no less than three SUVs until 2028, for example. They also got a 2026 Best of the Year Award for the Acura Integra, officially closed the chapter for their IMSA WeatherTech SportsCar Championship GTP with the swan song for their GTP program, and that was about all.
Luckily, the month isn’t over without an actual new model – even though it’s a pretty unique one. On October 24, 2026, they held an event at Vans HQ in Costa Mesa, California, and revealed a one-of-a-kind 2026 Acura ADX crossover SUV crafted in collaboration with extreme sports superstar and Vans athlete Marco ‘Coco’ Zurita. The professional Chilean BMX Vert and Mega Ramp athlete is also an entrepreneur and motorsports creator, so this collab isn’t really a surprise for his fans.
The multiple-time X-Games medalist, BMX World Champion, and the first rider in the world to land a triple tail-whip back in 2007 collaborated with Acura and Vans to create the bespoke ADX design drawing from the company’s sneakers and Zurita's passion for motorsports, street culture and custom fabrication, creating “distinctive design elements, materials and finishes that blend the creativity and energy of action sports with Acura's performance-driven automotive design.”
Available exclusively online at the Vans portal, Zurita's limited-edition Vans shoe is now up for grabs, but the same cannot be said about the one-of-a-kind 2026 Acura ADX SUV, unfortunately. On the outside, the ADX CZ-77 Concept mixes the tuning world with the BMX culture and comes with 19-inch Rotiform wheels and aero discs, a dedicated carbon fiber aerodynamic kit, bespoke fender flares, and a purpose-built rear BMX structure that can secure and display a BMX bike.
The graphics, of course, mirror the Vans x Coco Zurita shoe campaign. Moving inside, the ADX CZ-77 has Vans-inspired interior features like signature fabrics and design cues, with around 90% of the fabric used throughout the build provided directly by Vans North America, mirroring the brand's high-performance Skate and BMX footwear materials, thus celebrating both Zurita's 20th anniversary with Vans and Vans' own 60th anniversary.
In the past, Zurita, a native of Santiago, Chile, but now a resident of Los Angeles, partnered with Acura to build a custom 2023 Acura Integra first shown at the 2022 SEMA Show in Las Vegas, and they also had a 2024 Acura TLX Type S creation that was debuted at the 2024 Acura Grand Prix of Long Beach. Zurita even took up amateur drifting and has competed in the Unlimited AWD class at Global Time Attack.

As both Taysha Gene Therapies and Neurogene warm up for an important year of readouts, the Rett syndrome community is pinning hopes on a smooth finish—and possibly, a result in line with Novartis’ spinal muscular atrophy gene therapy Zolgensma.
Patients with Rett syndrome have historically had few treatment options—but 2027 could change that. Two gene therapies are at the FDA’s doorstep with strong data showing they can alter the trajectory of the rare neurodevelopmental disorder.
While experts are cautious to avoid using the word “cure,” the excitement is palpable. Monica Coenraads, founder and CEO of the Rett Syndrome Research Trust (RSRT), which previously helped to fund the academic science behind both Taysha’s and Neurogene’s candidates, made an optimistic comparison to Novartis’ spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) gene therapy Zolgensma.
“My hope is that something is so dramatic that we end up with a Zolgensma situation, where kids that would have been dead by two are taking ballet lessons,” Coenraads said. “You don’t need sophisticated statistics to understand that that was transformative.”
Zolgensma was greenlit by the FDA in 2019 as the first gene therapy for SMA after infants in Novartis’ Phase 1 START trial achieved motor milestones never seen before in the natural history of the disease, according to Novartis’ approval announcement .
Rett syndrome is a genetic neurodevelopmental disorder mainly affecting girls and women that causes a loss of motor and speech skills over time. In this space, it is now a “two-horse race” to bring a gene therapy to market, BMO Capital Markets analysts said. Candidates from Neurogene and Taysha Gene Therapies are each in the final stretch of late-stage development.
Taysha announced in August that it has completed dosing of TSHA-102 in 17 girls in the pivotal REVEAL trial that could support a regulatory submission in the first half of 2027. Neurogene has similarly completed dosing of its own gene therapy, NGN-401, in the registrational Embolden trial with data expected in the second half of 2027. The company has dosed 25 female patients three years and older in the Phase 3 trial, according to a June press release .
Rare diseases
FDA Signs Off on Neurogene’s ‘Best-Case Scenario’ Pivotal Study Design for Rett Syndrome
The pivotal trial for Neurogene’s Rett syndrome gene therapy makes use of baseline controls and a rigorous endpoint that could help ensure a broader label for the drug product, if approved, according to analysts.
July 1, 2025
·
2 min read
·
Tristan Manalac
Read more
Trials from both companies have demonstrated long-term efficacy from ongoing early-stage trials, with the one-time treatments resulting in 100% response rates—every patient met more than one developmental milestone.
For patients and caregivers in the Rett community, the headway marks a more hopeful period following many years with limited available treatments. Coenraads is the mother of Chelsea, a 30-year-old woman living with Rett syndrome who has never walked independently. Coenraads has witnessed her daughter’s lifetime of symptom-based medications and has seen this approach begin to give way to the potential for root-cause genetic treatments.
“It’s difficult to imagine a [small molecule] drug that works on a particular pathway having a dramatic effect on Rett syndrome, but if we could somehow target the root cause of the disease, the symptoms should go away,” Coenraads told BioSpace . “It was incredibly important for these companies to take these programs forward as the first genetic medicines to go to clinical trials,” she said, adding that this brought a lot of hope and excitement to the field.
With Taysha and Neurogene soon to be knocking on the regulatory door with their gene therapies, experts and caregivers are watching closely to determine whether both will find a place in the Rett syndrome landscape, with an eye particularly toward safety and long-term efficacy.
Finding an objective outcome
Originally described by Austrian physician Andreas Rett in the 1960s , Rett syndrome did not have an officially approved therapy until just a few years ago. In March 2023, Acadia Pharmaceuticals secured the regulatory greenlight for Daybue (trofinetide) for patients 2 years and older after the small molecule oral drug significantly improved Rett symptoms compared to placebo in the Phase 3 Lavender study .
In a testament to the difficulties of objectively assessing outcome measures in neurological conditions, Daybue entered the scene with some controversy concerning its efficacy in real-world settings. In a fact sheet written by RSRT leadership, including Coenraads, the organization noted that 61% of patients taking Daybue did not improve, while only 13% were rated as “much improved.”
Drug Development
Acadia Wins FDA Approval for First Rett Syndrome Medicine
Acadia Pharmaceuticals announced the approval of Daybue (trofinetide) as the first and only drug to treat Rett Syndrome, a rare, neurodegenerative disorder affecting primarily girls.
March 9, 2023
·
3 min read
·
Heather McKenzie
Read more
The Lavender and open-label Lilac-1 trials lacked data regarding specific symptoms, and adverse effects such as diarrhea and vomiting affected many patients, according to the RSRT’s findings. Acadia itself reported diarrhea in 82% of Daybue-treated patients vs. 20% of placebo comparators and vomiting in 29% on Daybue vs. 12% taking placebo.
Because of the challenges elicited by subjective outcomes, Coenraads is looking to gene therapies for a potential game-changing moment. For that, she takes cues from Zolgensma, with optimism that the data will speak for itself in a more objective manner.
Taysha and Neurogene
While Rett syndrome has been classified as a neurodevelopmental disorder, it is perhaps more accurately defined as a “neural network disorder” for the widespread effects of the central gene at its core, MECP2 , Sukumar Nagendran, head of R&D at Taysha, told BioSpace .
“ MECP2 is teleologically a very ancient gene and essentially acts as an orchestra conductor, controlling up to 4,000 genes in the central nervous system and elsewhere in the body,” Nagendran said. “That master orchestra conductor, which is the MECP2 gene, has fallen asleep in patients with Rett syndrome, and the orchestra doesn’t know what to do, but if the conductor wakes up, the music starts.”
Nagendran, who served as chief medical officer at AveXis—now Novartis Gene Therapies —during the development of Zolgensma, pointed to the similarities between that product and TSHA-102, particularly as both are one-time treatments.
“This program could be a very useful therapeutic option for patients with Rett syndrome and could transform the regulatory landscape if it works out that way,” leading to prioritization of single-arm comparators, Nagendran said. This could include natural history controls and comparisons to a patient’s own baseline—as is the case in Taysha’s REVEAL trial—to show individual patient progress. This would ensure a trial’s results don’t succumb to potential placebo effects, overcoming some of the objectivity challenges in the space.
TSHA-102 is delivered into the spinal cord, which BMO analysts said could provide a meaningful advantage for future uptake if approved, given the relative “ease of administration and common availability in the community” as compared with Neurogene’s therapy, which is delivered directly into the brain.
While Taysha and Neurogene are neck and neck in the race to bring the first gene therapy to patients with Rett syndrome, Neurogene has had the higher mountain to climb, particularly with regard to safety.
The company abandoned a higher dose of NGN-401 after a patient in its Phase 1/2 trial died. The death was attributed to the adeno-associated virus (AAV) used to deliver the genetic material. Neurogene subsequently built in a biomarker protocol to avoid further safety signals while also pursuing doses that would be effective, CEO Rachel McMinn told BioSpace .
Taysha’s gene therapy is also delivered via AAV, but has avoided the fatal safety issue that compromised Neurogene’s trial.
Despite the efficacy seen so far from these treatments, both McMinn and Nagendran are careful not to offer false hope.
“For CNS diseases, we are not in a place where it is remotely responsible to use the word ‘cure,’ McMinn said, “even though what we’re seeing are very encouraging signs of improvements. The gains in developmental milestones are very divergent from the natural history of the disease, and the promise [is] there, but there needs to be technological innovation to get closer to what you and I would truly consider a cure.”
She continued, “These girls seem to be markedly different little girls as they’ve been followed over time, but that doesn’t mean they’re going to college.”

This Camper Van Is Rugged Enough for Off-Road and Refined Enough for a Five-Star Stay
26 photos
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Ashben Conversions
Today's featured build is based on an AWD Mercedes-Benz Sprinter with a 170" wheelbase. It was brought to life by Ashben Conversions, a Sheffield, UK-based company that crafts bespoke homes on wheels.
As always, let's start by checking out the exterior – there are plenty of exterior upgrades done to this Sprinter. For starters, the vehicle rides on black Rogue Alloy wheels wrapped in General Grabber all-terrain tires. This is a great wheel and tire combo to complement the AWD capabilities.
At the front, Ashben installed two grille-mounted Lazer lights, as well as two Lazer lights and a deflector on the hood. On the opposite end, you'll come across a spare tire carrier / ladder combo, a step, and a cargo carrier.
The arguably most major exterior mod is on top of the van: an Atek pop-top roof tent. It has a three-piece fiberglass design and a weatherproof construction with three zipped windows.
It can accommodate a mattress size of 120 x 200 cm (approx. 47 x 79 inches). What's more, this unit comes with an integrated Maxxair vent fan and a 300 W solar panel on top.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Ashben Conversions The roof also holds a Thule Omnistor awning, a StarLink antenna, and a Dometic A/C unit. Other notable mods are power and water connections, side steps, and side pods.
Pods, also known as flares or capsules, are designed to increase the van width to allow you to fit a bed inside in an east to west arrangement instead of the standard north to south. This rig's Evo Design side pods are color matched to the van's paint and one of them comes with a half-slider window.
A single glance inside the van is enough to know you're dealing with a high-end space. The customer opted for a beautiful design comprised of laminated cabinetry with a wood grain finish, grey flooring, walls upholstered in grey Alcantara leather, and a matching ceiling with recessed LED light strips.
The look is complemented by red leather seat upholstery, a white solid surface countertop, and some black accents, like the kitchen hardware.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Ashben Conversions You'll notice that the interior has an open layout, with no wall separating the driver's cabin from the living space. Moreover, the driver and passenger seats have factory swivels, so they can be turned around to face the back of the van. You can also set up two swivel tables.
My favorite thing about this van's cabin setup is that it can be fully darkened. Specifically, the windshield and the two windows on the sides have Remis blinds that can block light from coming into the van.
The front seating area continues a bit further back in the form of a decently sized bench. Ashben even included an ottoman for resting your feet, which normally slots in between the driver and passenger seats when unused. It can also double as a step to get into bed.
Moreover, above, you'll find two cabinets and the pass-through that leads into the rooftop tent – you'll need a telescoping ladder to climb to it. A clever thing about the tent's design is that when it's lowered, the Maxxair vent fan slots in perfectly in the pass-through, allowing you to use it for the van's interior.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Ashben Conversions Next, we have a kitchen on the passenger side, by the entrance. It features a single-burner induction stovetop, a deep stainless steel sink with a cover, a coffee machine, an air fryer installed on a slide-out, a microwave oven, and a tall 130-liter Thetford fridge with a freezer compartment.
A large overhead cabinet and three drawers are available for storage in the kitchen. There's also a floor-to-ceiling unit next to the fridge that has a hanging closet and a cabinet with multiple shelves.
A bathroom sits on the opposite side, hidden behind a tall conventional door. What's more, to make sure no water splashes outside the bathroom, the builders added a retractable waterproof door.
The bathroom offers a shower with a handheld wand, an overhead cabinet, a counter with a small sink, and a bench-style toilet. My favorite part is its aesthetic, with wall panels that imitate stone.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Ashben Conversions Like in the majority of camper vans, you'll discover a fixed sleeping arrangement in the back of the living space, with a bed that's 6'2" (188 centimeters) long. The bedroom also boasts four overhead cabinets with recessed LED light strips underneath, two reading lights, and an A/C unit above.
A garage underneath the bed offers abundant storage space, both in terms of depth and height – the customer wanted the garage to have this much height so that they could haul mountain bikes.
You can access the garage from outside the van by opening the rear door and from inside through a small door under the bed. Moreover, there are L-Tracks integrated into the floor that allow you to secure your items.
The garage's sides are taken up by two boxes that accommodate the utility systems. Power is on the left side – the electrical system's highlights are a 628 Ah Fogstar battery bank and a 3,000 W inverter.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Ashben Conversions As for plumbing, the van is equipped with a freshwater tank, an under-mounted greywater tank, and an outdoor shower connection. There's one more important system: a Truma D4E Combi boiler that provides both heated air and hot water.
All in all, Ashben Conversions actually made this Sprinter van as comfortable as a simpler conventional home while also packing a welcoming design. The difference is that this home on wheels can take you on some wild adventures.

By Greg Amanatidis, Director of Marketing
26 October 2026
The company’s second Malaysian location puts it on Singapore’s doorstep and one of the world’s busiest trade corridors.
This week, Navia announced the opening of its freight forwarding office in Johor Bahru, Malaysia, continuing its expansion as a global player. This is its second location on the Malay Peninsula, its twelfth in APAC, and the next phase in its growth journey. The choice of Johor Bahru as a location was based on a few key factors: Singapore is on the doorstep, deeper coverage across Malaysia, and a relentless ambition for growth.
“Our expansion has always followed our customers…. Johor Bahru is us continuing to back the core markets that matter to them.”
Johor Bahru sits minutes from Singapore, connected by the world’s busiest land border crossing, with over 350,000 crossings a day (roughly four times the daily volume of San Diego–Tijuana’s San Ysidro crossing, which the U.S. Bureau of Transportation Statistics says is 87,569 crossings a day). A new rail link, opening later this year, will make that journey just five minutes.
The state is also home to Port Tanjung Pelepas, the world’s 15th-busiest seaport, handling over 14 million TEUs a year, and Senai International Airport. Since January 2025, the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ) has enabled duty-free trade and a single permit for land cargo moving between the two countries, targeting RM260 billion (approximately S$81 billion) in GDP for the zone, with 7% annual growth by 2030 according to Johor state government predictions.
In practice, that gives Navia customers a team with direct access to Singapore via sea and land. Take a shipment from Shanghai landing at Tanjung Pelepas: freight that once needed to clear through a third-party agent before reaching Singapore can now move under one Navia team, with one coordinated Navia solution, from origin port, to bonded storage, to final delivery. All of it is tracked with the same Critical Chain exception visibility and live reporting from the NaviaHub that Navia’s customers already use every day.
The new office extends Navia’s coverage across Malaysia. Alongside its existing Penang office, the Johor Bahru team now places Navia near Port Tanjung Pelepas, where a significant share of its freight already moves through.
The Johor Bahru office marks the second expansion Navia has made this year, following the launch of TCI Navia in China in August, another step in the company’s growing footprint.
“Our expansion has always followed our customers, not the other way round. We’ve been invested in Malaysia for seven years, and Johor Bahru is us continuing to back the core markets that matter to them. This is another step forward, not just for Malaysia but for what we’re building right across the region. What excites me most is the talent we’re adding on the ground and the capability we’re bringing in-house, so customers get the full Navia ecosystem working for them as one team.” , said Simon Borg, Group CEO of Navia.
About Navia:
Navia is a global freight forwarder and 3PL provider. Founded in Australia in 2003, Navia has grown into one of the largest independently-owned logistics providers in the market, with offices across Australia, China, Hong Kong, Malaysia, New Zealand and the United States. Being independently owned allows the Navia team to provide customers with the network and reach of a multi-national, coupled with the care and attention freight requires. All of this is backed by the NaviaHub proprietary platform, which gives customers real-time SLA reports and exception management down to the SKU-level. https://naviafreight.com

Google Quietly Releases Android Auto 18.1: How To Download and What's To Come
6 photos
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution/Google
Google has just started the rollout of another Android Auto build. This time, the new release is specifically aimed at users enrolled in the beta program, giving them the chance to take the update for a spin before it lands in the production channel.
Android Auto 18.1 beta lands without a changelog, so users who download the build will have to look for changes on their own.
At first glance, there are no front-facing changes in this update, at least compared to the previous update ( 18.0 stable ), so if you’re specifically interested in this part of the release, you won’t be getting any surprises. On the other hand, there’s a chance that the focus has been on what happens under the hood, and we all know that big things are taking place in this department.
How to download Android Auto 18.1 beta Our first stop is the download method. Because this new build is part of the beta program, you won’t see the download appearing as an automatic update in the Google Play Store unless you are enrolled in the program.
If you’re not, the only option is the manual download and installation.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution The process is not as complicated as it sounds, and it involves downloading the APK installer that you can use to update to Android Auto 18.1. This is a file that you just need to download on your device from this page . When the download is complete, tap the file and follow the on-screen wizard to finalize the update.
There are no complicated steps, and the only big requirement is enabling the installation of non-Google Play Store applications. This means you must configure your device to allow apps that aren’t published on the Play Store.
Big features planned for Android Auto While Android Auto 18.1 beta doesn’t bring any significant changes at first glance, we already know that many big things are on the radar for Google’s app.
This is why you can’t blame users when a new update comes out, though I’d say that some of these users aren’t necessarily excited about the new features but also about the chances of getting an update that finally fixes their issues with Android Auto.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution For example, Gemini has misbehaved in the most ridiculous ways since it landed on Android Auto in late 2025. Once the migration to Gemini was completed in September, and Google Assistant was retired , the Gemini struggle became an issue for all of these users, as they needed the default assistant to work correctly.
Users have complained about a wide variety of problems with Gemini, including the assistant not being able to call 911 or make regular phone calls. In some cases, Gemini was described by Android Auto users as another version of Cortana , Microsoft’s failed assistant that was launched for Windows Phone and Windows 10 users.
But leaving these struggles aside, there are big things to be excited about when it comes to the future of Android Auto.
The most important is the Cielo update, which includes a significant redesign of Android Auto and the introduction of new features like widgets and support for video apps.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution Cielo was announced in the spring of this year, and according to the most recent discoveries in Android Auto beta builds, it’s getting closer to the launch. However, it’s more unlikely to land in the remaining months of 2026, so the debut is now expected to take place in the first quarter of 2027.
Android Auto will receive widget support, allowing users to get access to certain information, such as the weather forecast and the next calendar entries, directly from the main Android Auto UI. This means the Coolwalk interface will get a redesign with the introduction of a new panel, as Google doesn’t want to go the CarPlay way and introduce a special screen just for widgets.
The video app support will allow users to watch their favorite clips directly on their infotainment screens. YouTube will be one of the apps that will go live on Android Auto as part of this update.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution Video apps will work only when vehicles are stationary, with apps that include an audio-only mode to support audio playback in the background once the vehicles start moving. Google is locking this ability behind a subscription, so you’ll need YouTube Premium for this feature.
Android Auto will also use the entire screen estate on infotainment units of various sizes and form factors. For example, most MINI models come with circular screens and right now display the Android Auto in a rectangular panel in the center of the unit. Once the Cielo update goes live, Android Auto will use the entire screen, with Google Maps expanding the maps to fill the screen and show more information.
The full build of today’s update is Android Auto 18.1.1643 beta.
